gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a 160 W total does not by itself keep the Mac's port at 140 W once a second device is plugged in: Notebookcheck lists the Anker Prime 160W's two-port split as 100 W + 60 W or 70 W + 70 W, and 100 W is the 20 V ceiling USB-IF says applied before the 28 V level existed.
standout_why: Compared against thegadgetmasters (cited), Macworld (cited), Apple Support 102378 (cited), thisusb, specsource, thunderboltlaptop and MacRumors. The basic mechanism is already on rival pages, so that part is not new: thisusb and specsource both say 140 W needs the 28 V level and a 240 W EPR cable, and thisusb prints the Anker 140W 4-port's 100 W + 40 W split and says the Mac's port 'drops to 100W or less, below the 140W line'. What none of them has: (1) a two-port split for any 160 W charger (thegadgetmasters and thunderboltlaptop only say 'read the allocation chart', Macworld prints only 65 W + 65 W (+30 W) for the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W and nothing for a laptop plus a phone); (2) the link between a '100 W' cell in a split table and the Mac being back on 20 V, off the 28 V contract; (3) GRL's description of how the 28 V mode is entered and lost. ChatGPT's first answer said a charger with more than 140 W total 'can be useful if you need to power a phone without sacrificing the MacBook's full allocation'; the one 160 W split I could source says otherwise. Standout is held at 2, not 3, because the Anker Prime split comes from a Notebookcheck news article (not a bench test, and Anker's own page prints only '160W Max'), and I could not read UGREEN's or AOHi's tables.
decides: It confirms that any pick works for the Mac alone: one port at 28 V / 5 A plus a MagSafe 3 cable (any 16-inch since 2021) or a 240 W EPR USB-C cable (Nov 2023 models or later, per Apple). It changes the second ranking figure, 'watts the laptop port keeps with a second device': that is 100 W on the Anker 140W 4-Port (Anker's table) and 100 W on the Anker Prime 160W (Notebookcheck), so neither keeps Apple's 140 W fast-charge pairing while a phone charges. The page must not credit the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W or the AOHi The Youth with keeping 140 W plus a phone until their own two-port tables are read; I could not open either store today. Apple's single-port adapter is the only candidate with no sharing at all. The map's top three are not overturned, but the tiebreak between them is unsourced for the two we link.

findings.label: Why 140 W is a 28 V figure and 100 W is a 20 V figure (USB-IF)
findings.value: 28 V fixed voltage enables up to 140 W; before PD 3.1 the limit was 100 W at 20 V / 5 A
findings.note: USB-IF's words: 'New 28V, 36V, and 48V fixed voltages enable up to 140W, 180W and 240W power levels, respectively.' and 'Prior to this update, USB PD was limited to 100W using a solution based on 20V using USB Type-C cables rated at 5A.' Arithmetic: 28 V x 5 A = 140 W; 20 V x 5 A = 100 W. So a port listed at 100 W in a split table is at 20 V or below, not on the 28 V level.

findings.label: How the 28 V mode is entered, and what the cable must report (Granite River Labs)
findings.value: The laptop (sink) asks to enter EPR mode; the cable's e-marker must be set 'EPR Mode Capable' and report 50 V and 5 A; on exit the voltage drops to 20 V or lower and the charger returns to SPR mode (100 W ceiling)
findings.source_title: USB Power Delivery Specification 3.1 (GRL technical blog, Cindy Chang, 2021-09-14)
findings.note: GRL is a USB test lab; this is its summary of the spec, not the spec PDF. Quotes: 'Sink sends EPR_Mode message, where the Data Object is set as Enter'; 'The E-Marker must be set to EPR Mode Capable and provide notification that it supports 50V and 5A'; 'Sink needs to transmit an EPR_KeepAlive message at specified intervals to maintain EPR mode'; 'the voltage should drop to 20V or lower'; SPR 'upper limit of 100W remain[s] unchanged'. Consequence: a 100 W (20 V / 5 A) e-marked cable has an e-marker but no EPR flag, so the charger never offers 28 V.
